newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Second day of fighting on Zaire-Rwanda border.
newsitem.headline: Second day of fighting on Zaire-Rwanda border.

text.p: Zairean and Rwandan soldiers traded artillery fire across their border early on Wednesday after Zaire warned Rwanda it would fight to defend its territory and its vast mineral wealth, aid workers said.
The two sides fought a mortar battle on Tuesday near the Rwandan border town of Cyangugu and aid workers in touch with the region reported more firing on Wednesday.
"There was a heavy exchange of artillery fire that lasted about two hours this morning. It is quiet right now," said Brenda Barton of the World Food Programme in Nairobi.
Barton, who spoke directly to contacts in Cyangugu, said one hotel in the town had been hit but she had no word of casualties.
"I understand there was a mortar which went right through the Hotel du Lac," she said.

For the first time since ethnic warfare erupted in eastern Zaire two weeks ago, Zairean and Rwandan soldiers on Tuesday exchanged sustained fire across the river that divides the two countries, fuelling the chaos that has driven half a million Rwandan and Burundian refugees from border camps inside Zaire.

"The worrying part about these 500,000 refugees is that there really is no assistance. We don't even know whether they have access to water," said U.N. refugee agency spokesman Panos Moumtzis from the Zairean town of Goma.
Even the refugees still in camps are receiving minimal food assistance because the U.N. is afraid that supplies will soon run out.
"The roads are blocked, nothing is coming in. We are really very anxious," said Moumtzis.
"Warehouses are very low in terms of food. Our understanding is that there is enough food for eight days...Right now what we are giving out is the absolute minimum to sustain life," he said.
U.N. sources said the United Nations was set to appoint Canada's ambassador to Washington, Raymond Chretien, as an interim representative on the crisis in eastern Zaire.

Fighting between Zairean troops and ethnic Tutsis, who first settled in what is now eastern Zaire some 200 years ago, threatens to draw in the Tutsi-dominated armies of Zaire's small neighbours Rwanda and Burundi.
Both deny Zairean accusations they back the Tutsi rebels, known as Banyamulenge, who have taken the town of Uvira and threaten to overrun the South Kivu provincial capital of Bukavu.
Zairean Foreign Minister Kitidwa Tumansi appeared on state television after the fighting to repeat Zaire's charges against Rwanda of territorial ambition.
"Zaire warns those who think the time has come to carve out new political and economic entities with hegemonic designs on its precious and strategic materials," Kitidwa said.
"If Rwanda persists in this dream it will be responsible for what happens in the Great Lakes sub-region," he added.
Zaire is rich in strategic minerals that virtually guaranteed Western support for its corrupt and inept government led by President Mobutu Sese Seko during the Cold War years.
At the weekend Mobutu, having treatment for cancer in Switzerland, sought to reassert his authority in Zaire's eastern borderlands by placing the two troubled Kivu provinces under military rule.
The fighting has created the most serious refugee crisis in Africa since apocalyptic massacres and civil war in Rwanda in 1994 sent two million people fleeing into nearby states.

Most of the latest refugees on the move are Rwandan Hutus. Thousands are former soldiers and militiamen and many took part in the 1994 massacre of up to a million minority Tutsis and their sympathisers in Rwanda before Tutsi rebels drove them out.
The refugees fear reprisals in Rwanda but a few have headed back home anyway, preferring that risk to violence in Zaire.
In Brussels, the European Union's aid commissioner Emma Bonino said one million people could die in Zaire. She accused the world of standing aloof from the tragedy.
